verses.commentary: The prophecy (massa, burden) that Habakkuk received. Unlike most prophets who speak to the people for God, Habakkuk speaks to God about the people. A dialogue between prophet and deity. The book models theological wrestling.

How long must I call and you do not listen? The classic lament question. Violence cried out, but no salvation comes. The prophet experiences what the Psalms describe. Unanswered prayer generates honest complaint.
Why make me see injustice? Why tolerate wrongdoing? Destruction, violence, strife, conflict abound. The prophet describes Judah's internal corruption. Evil is visible everywhere. God seems passive.
Law (torah) is paralyzed (or grows cold). Justice never prevails. The wicked surround the righteous. Justice comes out perverted. Social order inverted. Right and wrong no longer function as guides.
God responds. Look at the nations and watch. Be utterly amazed. Something is coming that you would not believe even if told. The answer will be unexpected. Divine response exceeds human imagination.

God raises up the Babylonians (Chaldeans). Ruthless and impetuous. They sweep across earth seizing homes not their own. The instrument of judgment is worse than those judged. This will be Habakkuk's next problem.

A feared and dreaded people. They are a law to themselves, promote their own honor. Autonomous, recognizing no authority. Self glorifying, self legislating. Terrifying precisely because they answer to no one but themselves.

Horses swifter than leopards, fiercer than wolves at dusk. Cavalry comes from afar, flies like eagles to devour. Animal imagery piles up: leopard speed, wolf ferocity, eagle swiftness. Nature's predators combined in human form.
All come for violence. Their hordes advance like desert wind. Prisoners gathered like sand. Countless captives, numberless as sand grains. Violence is their purpose, not a byproduct.
They mock kings, scoff at rulers. Fortified cities make them laugh. They build earthen ramps and capture them. No political power impresses them. No defenses hold. They conquer at will.

They sweep past like wind and go on. Guilty people whose strength is their god. Self worship. Power itself becomes deity. This is the heart of idolatry: making success the object of ultimate devotion.

Lord, are you not from everlasting? My God, my Holy One, you will never die. Habakkuk reasserts God's eternal nature. You appointed them for judgment, ordained them for punishment. The prophet acknowledges divine sovereignty even while questioning.

Eyes too pure to look on evil, cannot tolerate wrongdoing. Why then tolerate the treacherous? Why be silent while the wicked swallow the more righteous? The second complaint. The cure seems worse than the disease. Using evil to punish evil creates a new problem.
You made people like fish in the sea, like creatures without a ruler. Chaos and vulnerability. Humanity left exposed to predators. Where is divine protection? Where is cosmic order?

The wicked foe pulls all up with hooks, catches them in nets, gathers them in dragnets. He rejoices and is glad. Fishing imagery. Humanity as catch. The conqueror celebrates successful hunting of human prey.

He sacrifices to his net, burns incense to his dragnet. By these he lives in luxury, enjoys the choicest food. Net and dragnet worshipped because they produce results. Means become ends. Tools become gods. Success technology idolized.

Shall he keep emptying his net, destroying nations without mercy? The question hangs unanswered as chapter ends. Is there no limit to Babylonian conquest? Will ruthless power continue indefinitely? The prophet waits for God's reply.
